'''''Melilotus officinalis''''', known as '''sweet yellow clover''', '''yellow melilot''', '''ribbed melilot'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> and '''common melilot''', is a species of [[legume]] native to [[Eurasia]] and introduced in [[North America]], [[Africa]], and [[Australia]].<ref name=USDAFS>{{cite web|author=United States Forest Service|url=http://www.na.fs.fed.us/fhp/invasive_plants/weeds/yellow_sweetclover.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150928152822/http://www.na.fs.fed.us/fhp/invasive_plants/weeds/yellow_sweetclover.pdf |archive-date=2015-09-28 |url-status=dead |title=Yellow Sweetclover}}</ref>

==Description==
''Melilotus officinalis'' can be an annual or [[biennial plant]], and is {{convert|4|-|6|ft|cm|order=flip}} high at maturity.<ref name=USDAFS /> Leaves [[Phyllotaxis|alternate]] on the stem and possess three [[leaflet (botany)|leaflets]]. Yellow flowers bloom in spring and summer and produce fruit in pods typically containing one seed. Seeds can be viable for up to 30 years. Plants have large taproots and tend to grow in groups.<ref name=USDAFS /> Plants have a characteristic sweet odor.<ref name=USDAFS />

==Identification==
[[File:Melilotus officinalis keels.jpg|thumb|The lower petal is shorter than the lateral ones in ribbed melilot.]]
Ribbed melilot is very similar in appearance to some other melilots, particularly [[Melilotus altissimus|tall melilot]]. Its fruits, however, are ribbed and glabrous (not hairy), the upper leaflets are more broadly oval, and the keel, or lower petal, is slightly shorter than the side petals (same length in tall melilot).<ref name=Rose>{{cite book |last1=Rose |first1=Francis |title=The Wild Flower Key |date=2006 |publisher=Frederick Warne |location=London|isbn=978-0-7232-5175-0}}</ref><ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |publisher=C&M Floristics |edition=4th |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref>

==Habitat==
[[File:20140613Melilotus officinalis.jpg|thumb]]
''M. officinalis'' is native to Europe and Asia and has been introduced to North America as a forage crop.<ref name=USDAFS /> It commonly grows in [[calcareous]] loamy and clay soils with a pH above 6.5 and can tolerate cold temperatures and drought; it does not tolerate standing water<ref name=USDAFS /> or acidic soils, with a pH of 5.5 as the plant's lowest limit.<ref name=NRCS /> Common places where it can be found include open disturbed land, prairies, and savannas, and it grows in full or partial sunlight. It is an [[invasive species]] in areas where it has been introduced, especially in open grasslands and woodlands where it shades and outcompetes native plant species.<ref name=USDAFS />

==Toxicology==
Sweet clover contains coumarin that converts to [[dicoumarol]], which is a powerful [[anticoagulant]] toxin, when the plant becomes moldy. This can lead to bleeding diseases (internal hemorrhaging) and death in cattle. Consequently, hay containing the plant must be properly dried and cured, especially in wet environments.<ref>{{cite web |author1=Nicole Kresge |author2=Robert D. Simoni |author3=Robert L. Hill |name-list-style=amp |title=Hemorrhagic Sweet Clover Disease, Dicumarol, and Warfarin: the Work of Karl Paul Link |access-date=2009-08-11 |url=http://www.jbc.org/cgi/content/full/jbc;280/8/e5 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120802114042/http://www.jbc.org/cgi/content/full/jbc;280/8/e5 |url-status=dead |archive-date=August 2, 2012 }}</ref><ref name=NRCS />

==Uses==
The seeds are eaten by game birds, including grouse.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Niering |first1=William A. |author-link1=William Niering| last2=Olmstead |first2=Nancy C. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers, Eastern Region |year=1985 |orig-year=1979|publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50432-1 |page=535}}</ref>

Sweetclover can be used as pasture or livestock feed when properly cured.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Reiner|first=Ralph E.|title=Introducing the Flowering Beauty of Glacier National Park and the Majestic High Rockies|publisher=Glacier Park, Inc.|year=1969|pages=52}}</ref> It is most palatable in spring and early summer, but livestock may need time to adjust to the bitter taste of [[coumarin]] in the plant. Prior to [[World War II]], before the common use of commercial agricultural fertilizers, the plant was commonly used as a cover crop to increase nitrogen content and improve subsoil water capacity in poor soils.<ref name=NRCS /> It is the most drought-tolerant of the commercially available legumes.<ref>{{cite web |author1=Dan Ogle |author2=Loren St. John |author3=Mark Stannard |author4=Larry Holzworth |name-list-style=amp |url=https://www.plants.usda.gov/pmpubs/pdf/idpmctn240103.pdf |title=Grass, Grass-like, Forb, Legume, and Woody Species for the Intermountain West |access-date=2019-01-31 |archive-date=2016-12-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161228201424/http://plants.usda.gov/pmpubs/pdf/idpmctn240103.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> Sweet clover is a [[Northern Nectar Sources for Honeybees|major source of nectar]] for domestic [[honey bee]]s as hives near sweetclover can yield up to 200 pounds of honey in a year.<ref name=NRCS>{{cite web|author=USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service|url=https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_DOCUMENTS/nrcs144p2_043029.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150624043752/http://www.nrcs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_DOCUMENTS/nrcs144p2_043029.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=June 24, 2015|title=Yellow Sweetclover & White Sweetclover}}</ref>

Sweetclover has been used as a [[phytoremediation]]—phytodegradation plant for treatment of soils contaminated with [[Dioxins and dioxin-like compounds|dioxins]].<ref>[https://docs.google.com/viewer?a=v&pid=gmail&attid=0.1&thid=1381098a3beff9d9&mt=application/pdf&url=https://mail.google.com/mail/?ui%3D2%26ik%3D374c5f005d%26view%3Datt%26th%3D1381098a3beff9d9%26attid%3D0.1%26disp%3Dsafe%26zw&sig=AHIEtbQSOrpBwC3n7T_xGoUf2NgQq0_02g Sandia National Labs: SSFL Report; pg.10] . accessed 6.12.2012</ref>

In the chemical industry, dicoumarol is extracted from the plant to produce [[rodenticide]]s.<ref name=NRCS />

==Management==
When ''M. officinalis'' is invasive, it can be managed by mulching, hand-pulling, mowing, or herbicide applications (e.g., [[2,4-Dichlorophenoxyacetic acid|2,4-D]]) before flowering. Prescribed burns in late fall or early spring followed by another burn in late spring can reduce the number of plants before seed set.<ref name=USDAFS />
